group.title: Describing situations
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: Not safe or steady, and likely to get worse or fall.
examples: The company’s finances are in a {precarious} state.
wrong: The bridge was precarious, so it was completely safe and solid.

words.meaning: Extremely serious or bad.
examples: The town is in {dire} need of clean water.
wrong: The situation was dire, so nobody needed any help.

words.meaning: Full of worry, tension or problems.
examples: The talks were {fraught} with difficulty.
wrong: The meeting was fraught, so everyone felt relaxed and happy.

words.meaning: Very serious, worrying and without hope.
examples: The doctor’s report was {grim}.
wrong: The news was grim, so everyone celebrated.

words.meaning: Harmful or bad for someone or something.
examples: Bad weather had an {adverse} effect on the harvest.
wrong: The adverse conditions helped the plants grow better than ever.

words.meaning: Most common or strongest at a particular time.
examples: The {prevailing} view is that prices will rise.
wrong: The prevailing opinion is one that almost nobody holds.

words.meaning: Not expected or predicted before it happened.
examples: The flight was canceled due to {unforeseen} problems.
wrong: The problem was unforeseen, so we had planned for it for months.

words.meaning: Making you feel worried that something will be too difficult.
examples: Starting a new job abroad can be {daunting}.
wrong: The task was daunting, so I felt sure it would be easy.

words.meaning: Slightly worried or uncomfortable about a situation.
examples: There was an {uneasy} silence after his remark.
wrong: She felt uneasy, completely calm and at peace.

words.meaning: Full of sudden change, conflict or disorder.
examples: The country went through a {turbulent} decade.
wrong: It was a turbulent year, calm and without any change.

words.meaning: Very dangerous and likely to cause harm.
examples: The climbers made a {perilous} journey across the ice.
wrong: The perilous path was the safest way home.

words.meaning: Making it easy for something good to happen.
examples: A quiet room is {conducive} to study.
wrong: The loud, crowded room was very conducive to sleep.

words.meaning: Happening at a good or convenient time.
examples: This is an {opportune} moment to ask for a raise.
wrong: It was an opportune moment, so it was the worst possible time.

words.meaning: Very hard to solve, control or deal with.
examples: Traffic in the city is an {intractable} problem.
wrong: The problem was intractable, so we solved it in a minute.

words.meaning: Lasting much longer than expected or usual.
examples: After {protracted} negotiations, they signed the deal.
wrong: The talks were protracted, lasting only a few seconds.

words.meaning: About to happen very soon.
examples: Dark clouds warned of an {imminent} storm.
wrong: The storm is imminent, so it won’t arrive for years.

words.meaning: Going to happen soon, usually something bad.
examples: Everyone talked about the {impending} layoffs.
wrong: The impending crisis ended a long time ago.

words.meaning: Changing a lot and not calm or decided.
examples: The weather will stay {unsettled} all week.
wrong: Things were unsettled, so everything was calm and decided.

words.meaning: Not growing, changing or moving forward.
examples: Wages have been {stagnant} for years.
wrong: The economy was stagnant, growing faster than ever.

words.meaning: Moving or developing more slowly than normal.
examples: Sales were {sluggish} in the first quarter.
wrong: The market was sluggish, racing ahead at record speed.

words.meaning: Doing well, with prices or activity rising.
examples: The housing market remains {buoyant}.
wrong: Demand was buoyant, so nobody wanted to buy anything.

words.meaning: Not active now, but able to become active again later.
examples: The volcano has been {dormant} for centuries.
wrong: The dormant project is the busiest one in the office.

words.meaning: Likely to change quickly and not fixed.
examples: The situation is {fluid}, so we’ll update you hourly.
wrong: The plans are fluid, so they will never change.

words.meaning: Unclear and hard to understand, often in a suspicious way.
examples: The details of the deal remain {murky}.
wrong: The rules were murky, so everyone understood them clearly.

words.meaning: Very loud, busy or full of disorder and excitement.
examples: The singer got a {tumultuous} welcome.
wrong: The tumultuous crowd sat in total silence.

words.meaning: Extremely upsetting and frightening to experience.
examples: Survivors described their {harrowing} escape.
wrong: It was a harrowing day, relaxing and pleasant from start to finish.

words.meaning: Very tiring and demanding a lot of effort over a long time.
examples: The climbers faced a {grueling} ten-hour ascent.
wrong: The grueling race was so easy that nobody felt tired.

words.meaning: Needing a lot of hard work and effort.
examples: Rebuilding the town was an {arduous} task.
wrong: The arduous job took no effort at all.

words.meaning: Slow and difficult to use or manage because it is large or complicated.
examples: The old booking system is {cumbersome}.
wrong: The cumbersome process was quick and simple.

words.meaning: Unusual and unexpected in a way that causes problems.
examples: The trip went smoothly with nothing {untoward}.
wrong: Something untoward happened, so everything went normally.

words.meaning: Unfortunate and making you wish it had not happened.
examples: The delay was {regrettable} but unavoidable.
wrong: The mistake was regrettable, so we’re glad it happened.

words.meaning: Very bad and deserving strong disapproval.
examples: The prisoners lived in {deplorable} conditions.
wrong: The hotel was deplorable, so we gave it five stars.

words.meaning: Very poor in quality, or making you feel sad.
examples: The team’s {dismal} season ended in last place.
wrong: Their dismal results put them at the top of the league.

words.meaning: Tense and unfriendly, showing that people are not relaxed.
examples: Relations between the neighbors are {strained}.
wrong: The talks were strained, so everyone felt relaxed and friendly.

words.meaning: Friendly and without anger or argument.
examples: They reached an {amicable} agreement.
wrong: The divorce was amicable, full of shouting and anger.

words.meaning: Polite and friendly, especially in a formal way.
examples: The two leaders had a {cordial} meeting.
wrong: The meeting was cordial, so they insulted each other loudly.

words.meaning: Hard to live in because the conditions are harsh.
examples: The desert is an {inhospitable} place.
wrong: The island was inhospitable, so it was perfect for living.

words.meaning: Very common and widespread, usually of something bad.
examples: Rumors were {rife} in the office.
wrong: Crime is rife, so it almost never happens here.

words.meaning: Not strict or careful enough about rules or standards.
examples: Security at the gate was {lax}.
wrong: The rules were lax, so every small mistake was punished.

words.meaning: Needing to be dealt with immediately.
examples: We have more {pressing} matters to discuss.
wrong: It’s a pressing issue, so it can wait for years.
